note: Symbol glossary for the study notes. Lookup: chapter symbols, then common. A list gives context variants; 'when' is a regex tested on the nearest text first (sentence or formula line, then block, then section heading). 'terms' are clinical example terms, shown in clinical and medical sections; 'case': true matches the exact spelling only.

Δx.n: sideways shift of the top face

terms.d: Healthy bone has a large Young's modulus Y, so a large stress gives only a small strain. It is stiff and resists deformation.
Bone loses mineral and density, so its structure is weaker and less stiff, with a lower Y. It breaks under stresses that healthy bone can carry.
An inherited collagen disorder, also called brittle bone disease. The bone has lower strength and fractures easily.

P_G.n: gauge pressure of the liquid column

F_in.n: input force on the small piston

F_out.n: output force on the large piston

h.n: height of the fluid column or depth

terms.d: A blood pressure cuff. It reads pressure in mmHg, the height of a mercury column the pressure could hold up.
Blood pressure is a gauge pressure: the amount above atmospheric pressure. A reading of 120 mmHg means 120 mmHg more than the surrounding air.
Pascal's principle: pressure on a confined fluid is passed on equally, so a small force on a small piston gives a large force on a large piston.
Fat is less dense than muscle and bone. Weighing a person in air and under water gives the buoyant force, then body density and body fat.

Q.n: flow rate: mass flow in kg/s or volume flow in m³/s

ℓ.n: distance the fluid moves in time t

terms.d: Blood flows in smooth parallel layers, laminar flow, fastest in the centre of the vessel.
Continuity, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂: the smaller area makes the blood flow faster there, and the flow often becomes turbulent.
A narrowed segment of an artery. By continuity, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, the smaller area makes the blood flow faster there, and the flow often becomes turbulent.
Blood forced through a narrowed or damaged valve flows fast and becomes turbulent. The turbulence makes the sound heard as a murmur.
A sound heard with a stethoscope. It is made by turbulent blood flow, for example through a narrowed or damaged valve.
The blood supply reaching the tissue. Turbulence wastes energy in sideways motion, so less blood reaches the tissue.

T.n: wall stress when written T = Pₜ × R / μ

Tₒ.n: wall tension of the normal vessel

μ.n: wall thickness, another symbol for t

y.n: distance between the plates, the thickness of the fluid layer

D.n: diameter of the vessel or tube

r.n: radius of the alveolus or sphere
radius of the tube or vessel

L.n: length of the line on the surface

F.n: viscous force needed to slide the plate

v̄.n: average flow speed in the tube

P.n: pressure inside the vessel or alveolus

terms.d: Continuity, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂: the narrowed artery has a smaller area, so the blood flows faster through it.
A narrowed carotid artery in the neck. The blood speeds up through it by continuity, its pressure falls by Bernoulli, and the flow drops sharply by Poiseuille.
Bernoulli's principle: a fast jet of oxygen through a narrow opening has a low pressure, which draws in room air. The size of the opening sets a precise oxygen mix.
Poiseuille's law: flow depends on the vessel radius to the fourth power, r⁴. A small narrowing cuts flow sharply, so a higher pressure is needed to keep the same flow.
Too many red blood cells make the blood thicker, so its viscosity is higher and it flows with more resistance.
Too few red blood cells make the blood less viscous, so it flows more easily, but it carries less oxygen.
Flow through a narrowed or damaged valve is fast and turbulent, with a high Reynolds number. The turbulence makes the sound.
Laplace's law, T = P × r: the bulge has a wider radius, so its wall tension is higher. The higher tension stretches the wall further, so the bulge keeps growing.
Premature babies may not make enough surfactant. Surface tension stays high, so by P = 2T/r small alveoli collapse and breathing is hard.
Respiratory distress syndrome: without enough surfactant, surface tension stays high and small alveoli collapse, so breathing is hard. It affects premature babies.
Without enough surfactant, surface tension stays high and small alveoli collapse, so breathing is hard. It affects premature babies.
A substance made in the lungs that lowers the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli, so they stay open with less pressure.
Blood rises into a thin capillary tube by itself, because adhesion to the glass and surface tension pull it up.
Fatty plaque builds up in the artery wall and narrows it. By continuity the blood speeds up in the narrow part, and by Bernoulli its pressure there falls.
Deep vein thrombosis: a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg. Doppler ultrasound shows where the flow is blocked or slowed.
Transient ischaemic attack: a short-lived lack of blood to part of the brain, for example when a narrowed carotid artery greatly reduces the flow.
The flow through the cannula depends on its radius to the fourth power, r⁴, so a slightly wider cannula gives a much faster infusion.
High blood pressure. By Laplace's law, T = P × r, a higher pressure raises the tension in the vessel wall.
The largest artery, with a large radius and a high pressure. By Laplace's law its wall tension is high, so it needs a thick, strong wall.
Ultrasound reflected from moving red blood cells comes back at a shifted frequency. The shift gives the speed and direction of blood flow.

v.n: speed of sound or of the wave

v_D.n: speed of the detector or observer

terms.d: Ultrasound reflected from moving red blood cells comes back at a shifted frequency. The shift gives the speed and direction of blood flow.
Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy: shock waves made outside the body are focused on a kidney stone and break it into small pieces that can pass out in the urine.
A vibrating tuning fork is held near the ear or placed on a bone to test hearing and the sense of vibration.
The thermometer stays in contact with the body until both reach the same temperature. By the zeroth law its reading is then the body temperature.
Normal body temperature is about 37 °C = 98.6 °F = 310 K. A fever is a temperature above about 38 °C.
X-rays and CT use ionizing radiation, which can damage cells. Ultrasound uses sound waves and does not ionize.

v.n: speed of light in the medium

F.n: focal point of the mirror or lens

terms.d: A thin, flexible bundle of optical fibres. One bundle carries light in and another carries the image out by total internal reflection, so organs are seen without open surgery.
A thin, flexible bundle of optical fibres. One bundle carries light in and another carries the image out by total internal reflection, so organs are seen without open surgery.
Optical fibres carry laser light by total internal reflection to the exact spot where tissue is cut or sealed.
A lens prescription gives the power in dioptres, P = 1/f with f in metres: + for a converging, convex lens and − for a diverging, concave lens.

θ.n: angle the image fills at the eye

θ₀.n: angle the object fills at the eye without the lens

I₁.n: first image, made by the objective lens

I₂.n: final image, made by the eyepiece

Fₒ.n: focal point of the objective lens

F.n: focal point of the mirror or lens

terms.d: Laser eye surgery that reshapes the cornea. The cornea does most of the eye's refraction, so changing its curve corrects myopia or hyperopia.
With age the eye lens stiffens and cannot focus close up, so the near point moves farther away. Convex reading glasses help.
Myopia: the eye focuses light in front of the retina. A diverging, concave lens with negative power moves the focus back onto the retina.
Hyperopia: the eye focuses light behind the retina. A converging, convex lens with positive power moves the focus forward onto the retina.
A focused laser beam cuts tissue and its heat seals small blood vessels at the same time, so there is little bleeding.
A focused laser beam cuts tissue and its heat seals small blood vessels at the same time, so there is little bleeding.
Photocoagulation: laser heat clots the blood and seals or blocks leaking vessels in the retina, for example in diabetic retinopathy.
Laser heat clots the blood and seals or blocks the vessel, for example leaking retinal vessels in diabetic retinopathy.
Laser light is intense and directional. The eye can focus it to a tiny spot on the retina and burn it, so goggles made for that laser are worn.

Kₘₐₓ.n: maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electron

N₀.n: number of nuclei at the start

α.n: alpha particle: a helium-4 nucleus, 2 protons and 2 neutrons

β.n: beta particle: an electron, β⁻, or a positron, β⁺

γ.n: gamma ray: a high-energy photon with no charge and no mass

terms.d: Ionizing radiation kills tumour cells. Rotating the source around the patient keeps the tumour in the beam all the time, while each part of the healthy tissue gets only a small dose.
Gamma rays have no charge and penetrate deeply, so they can reach tumours deep in the body. Staff are protected by lead shielding.
A tracer with a short half-life gives enough radiation for imaging, then decays away quickly, so the patient's dose stays low.
A Geiger-Müller counter detects and counts ionizing radiation, so it shows where radioactive material has spread. It cannot tell which type of radiation it is.
A Geiger-Müller counter detects and counts ionizing radiation, so it shows where radioactive material has spread. It cannot tell which type of radiation it is.
Absorbed dose is recorded in gray, 1 Gy = 1 J/kg. Dose equivalent in sievert, dose × QF, allows for the type of radiation and so shows the biological risk.
Dose limits cap the radiation a worker may receive: 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years by the IAEA, and 50 mSv, 5 rem, per year by the US NRC.
Living things take in carbon-14. After death it decays with a half-life of about 5730 years, so the C-14 left shows the age.
Alpha particles are stopped by paper or the skin, but inside the body they put all their energy into a small volume of tissue and do great damage.
Electrocardiogram: electrodes on the skin record the potential differences made by the heart's electrical activity.
Electroencephalogram: electrodes on the scalp record the potential differences made by brain activity.
A high voltage can drive a large current through the body. The current can disturb the heart rhythm and burn tissue.
Body tissue resists current like any conductor, R = ρL/A. Dry skin has a high resistance, so gel is used to give electrodes good contact.
At rest the inside of the cell is about −70 mV. Na⁺ flowing in depolarizes the membrane and K⁺ flowing out repolarizes it; this is the action potential.
The myelin sheath around nerve fibres is damaged, so nerve signals travel more slowly or are blocked.
An insulating fatty sheath around nerve fibres. It makes nerve signals travel much faster.

Magnetic resonance imaging uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves, not ionizing radiation, and shows soft tissue in detail. The magnet pulls hard on metal objects, so metal is dangerous near the scanner.
Magnetoencephalography: measures the tiny magnetic fields made by electric currents in the brain.
Magnetocardiography: measures the magnetic fields made by the heart's electrical activity.
